learningObjective: Explain how a serving scheduler handles KV cache pressure via preemption / swap-out and its trade-offs.
stem: In a serving system running near KV-cache capacity, a burst of new prefill requests arrives. Which description of the scheduler's response is correct for vLLM-style continuous batching + paged KV?

options.text: The scheduler admits all new requests immediately and rewrites older sequences' KV cache in-place with the new prefill data; this is safe because older KV entries can always be recomputed later at negligible cost by re-prefilling those sequences.

The scheduler preempts one or more ongoing sequences (typically the ones with least urgency by policy) — either dropping their KV cache to be recomputed later, or swapping their KV blocks to host memory — and admits the new prefills into the freed KV blocks. Preempted sequences are resumed when capacity is available; this trades their added latency for aggregate throughput.

The scheduler compacts the KV cache by moving all blocks to contiguous memory, which frees up fragmented space for the new prefills; this defragmentation is fast because it uses async DMA copies within HBM.
The scheduler rejects all new requests until the cache pressure drops; ongoing decode continues unaffected. New requests receive an HTTP 503 response after a short timeout.

explanation: Modern schedulers (Orca-inspired, implemented in vLLM/SGLang/TRT-LLM) manage KV cache pressure via preemption: when a new prefill's KV requirement plus existing KV exceeds capacity, the scheduler preempts (evicts or swaps to host memory) some ongoing sequences to admit new work. Recomputation-on-resume vs swap-to-host is a policy choice: recompute is simple but pays prefill cost twice for the preempted sequences; swap-to-host avoids recompute at the cost of PCIe traffic. Both policies are needed depending on prompt length and PCIe bandwidth.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: in-place overwrite would corrupt other sequences.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: preempt-and-resume with recompute or swap.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: paged KV avoids external fragmentation by design; compaction is not necessary.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: outright rejection is a coarse and suboptimal response.

assumptions: Paged KV cache with a block-level allocator.
Scheduler is aware of per-request KV footprint and priorities.
nonImplications: Does not imply preemption is free; it adds tail latency to preempted requests.
Does not imply every serving stack chooses the same preemption policy.

distractorRationales.C: Paged KV eliminates external fragmentation, making compaction unnecessary.

performanceClaim.scope: Serving scheduler preemption behavior under KV cache pressure
